content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper aims to reduce the complexity of the encoder in neural video compression. The proposed approach encodes frames independently and then uses motion estimation on the receiver side to produce reconstructions. As shown in Fig 1.c, this is achieved by 1) encoding a frame into a representation \hat y, 2) recovering a reconstruction \hat x given \hat y and \bar y, where \bar y is obtained by interpolating two previously transmitted frames. The authors claim speed-ups at inference time as well as good R-D performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
While the overall approach is interesting and I appreciate the effort to reduce encoder complexity, I see various weaknesses spread throughout the paper

W1) Overall setup and achieved performance. I am very surprised by the rate-distortion performance, and I cannot see any explanation for the low rates we achieve. After all, the encoder transform "WZ Encoder Net" does not see anything except the current frame. By design, the only way to leverage temporal redundancies is on the decoder side via the side information loop. However, this means that the encoder never knows what the decoder will have access to. I thus do not see any way it could in general learn to reduce bitrate by any significant margin.
- How could the encoder know which information is novel and needs to be transmitted?
- When looking at Fig 1, top row, we see the representation \hat y contains a lot of information about the image. How could the rate of the model then be lower than just an image compression model? You also mention you compare to Minnen et al's I-frame model. Are you fine-tuning them for your task? Otherwise, the "Minnen2022" Results in Fig. 6 seem really off.
FWIW, an image compression model will have about 3x the rate shown. Please enlighten me how the proposed scheme could achieve these results, without a temporal entropy model. 

W2) Speed Results. While the results in Table 2 are promising, various important comparisons are missing. First and foremost I am missing "ELF-VC" (Rippel et al, ICCV 2021). Despite using flow on the encoder side, they achieve 10 FPS encoding and 18 FPS decoding on a Titan V, while reporting 44.3% BD-rate reduction over H.264 on UVG. In contrast, the proposed method achieves only either 32% BD-rate reduction at about 2.9FPS encoding, or 24.3% BD-rate reduction at 5.5 FPS, thus being both slower and worse in R-D. (It's unfortunately unclear what the authors used to measure GPU speed, possibly the NVIDIA RTX A5000 they used for training, which is a better GPU than the Titan V).
Further note that the proposed methods uses future frames for frame interpolation, whereas ELF-VC is only operating in the P-frame mode, which means the ELF-VC numbers are even more impressive.

W3) (minor) H.264, H.265 configs: The authors use ffmpeg using both `veryfast` and `-tune zerolatency` as well as various additional parameters (C.1), which puts the codecs at a disadvantage.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I struggled with the exposition since Fig 1b) is somewhat irrelevant for the actual method. Linking the proposed method to distributed source coding seems a bit weird to me. The main figures are clear though.

As mentioned above, I am not convinced I could reproduce the results since I do not understand why we would be able to get these results.
content.summary_of_the_review: As mentioned above, I am skeptical of the results since I see no intuitive explanation for why an independent encoder could achieve low rates without seeing the decoder loop. Please provide a) some intuition on what happens if you train your models. An interesting thing to think about is what happens with Minnen et al's model if you put it into your scheme. Also, b), describe how the bitrates are calculate. Which ANS implementation do you use?

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a low-complexity video compression method based on the distributed video coding architecture. The proposed solution does not rely on the motion estimation/compensation on the encoder side and only performs intra feature extraction. At the same time, the proposed approach used the decoded frames to interpolate the to-be-reconstructed frame, and then the intra feature and the interpolated frames are fused to obtain the final reconstructed frames. Results show that the proposed solution is much faster than the previous learning-based frame and achieves similar RD performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

The proposed distributed learned video compression is interesting and results also show that it has a lot of advantages over the existing learning-based video codecs. The speed is much faster and we can use a very lightweight encoder, which is very useful in a lot of scenarios. 

**Weaknesses**

1. The comparison between the proposed method and DVC or DCVC is not fair enough. DVC and DCVC follow the low delay settings where they only used one previous frame as the reference frame to obtain the motion compensation results. However, the proposed method needs two adjacent frames to generate the final reconstructed frames.  Therefore, the authors are suggested to compare with other B frame based learned video compression methods.

2. It seems like the proposed method cannot be easily extended for the low delay setting. In other words, the proposed framework is not very general and may be limited in some scenarios. 

3. The proposed solution is only evaluated on the UVG and MCL datasets while the video coding community usually uses the CTC dataset, like Class A/B/C/D/E/F.  For the UVG dataset, it is a high frame rate video dataset and it is easier to use the frame interpolation method to generate the reconstructed frames, which means the distributed dvc is expected to perform better on these datasets.  However, for the commonly used dataset like Class B or Class C, it brings a lot of challenges for the frame interpolation method. The authors should provide more discussion. Besides, the GoP is set as 8 in experiments while I think if we set the GoP as 10 or  20, the performance may be not satisfactory since the distance is larger. 

4. The proposed method uses existing modules like RIFE to implement the whole framework and the technical contribution may not strong enough.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed distributed DVC is somewhat new and enjoys faster inference at a similar performance. The writing and organization of this paper are clear enough.  It seems it is possible to reproduce the proposed methods.
content.summary_of_the_review: In my opinion, it is a borderline paper. The proposed idea is somewhat new and results on UVG dataset are encouraging. However, the evaluation is not sufficient(see the weakness) and I doubt whether the proposed method also works on other widely used datasets.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a neural network-based video codec framework for resource-constrained devices. The basic idea is to use the WZ codec to move the computation-heavy operations from the encoder to the decoder and then replaces conventional codec components with neural network to make the framework end-to-end trainable. The authors also avoid using the feedback channel between the encoder and decoder by using a channel-wise auto-regressive entropy model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
This paper combines multiple recent works in a new end-to-end framework.

Weakness:
1. The performance is not impressive.
2. No comparison for the decoder overhead.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. The writing clarity is not very good. 
2. The novelty is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review:
1. The performance is below deep video compression with the predictive coding architecture. Also, the performance does not have much advantage over conventional codecs like H.264 or H.265.

2. This paper aims to simplify the encoder at the cost of a more complicated decoder, but there is no comparison between the proposed decoder complexity and benchmark solutions. According to Figure 13, the decoder is very heavy and should be much heavier than H.264 or H.265.

3. The writing clarity is not very good. For example, it is unclear how the quantization is handled during training. The authors mentioned that "the quantizer is replaced with an additive uniform noise for learning entropy model, and a rounded tensor with straight-through gradient replaces the noise one to flow to the WZ decoder." Why use uniform noise of entropy model and STE for the WZ decoder? What is the "noise one"?

4. The novelty is limited, as this work is a combination of multiple recent works in an end-to-end framework.

5. The evaluation only uses high-resolution datasets. But the application scenario is mainly for resource-constrained devices, which may use low-resolution video like 640x480 more often.

content.title: Low-complexity Deep Video Compression with A Distributed Coding Architecture
content.TL;DR: We design the first end-to-end distributed deep video compression framework based on the distributed coding paradigm, which outperforms traditional distributed video codecs and achieves competitive performance with H.264.
content.abstract: Prevalent video compression methods follow a $predictive\;coding$ architecture that relies on a heavy encoder to exploit the statistical redundancy, which makes it challenging to deploy them on resource-constrained devices. Meanwhile, as early as the 1970s, distributed source coding theory, namely, Slepian-Wolf and Wyner-Ziv theorems, has indicated that efficient compression of correlated sources can be achieved by exploiting the source statistics at the decoder only, with the help of effective side information (SI). This has inspired a $distributed\;coding$ architecture that is promising to reduce the encoder complexity. While there have been some attempts to develop practical distributed video coding systems, traditional methods suffer from a substantial performance gap to the predictive coding architecture. Inspired by the recent successes of deep learning in enhancing image and video compression, we propose the first end-to-end distributed deep video compression (Distributed DVC) framework with neural network-based modules that can be optimized to improve the rate-distortion performance. A key ingredient is an effective SI generation module at the decoder, which helps to effectively exploit the inter-frame correlation without computation-intensive encoder-side motion estimation and compensation. Experiments show that Distributed DVC significantly outperforms conventional distributed video coding methods and H.264. Meanwhile, it enjoys $6\sim7$ times encoding speedup against DVC with only 1.61\% increase in the bitrate for 1080P test videos on the UVG dataset.
